```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 150,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

Snake plots display data as horizontal bands in a serpentine layout — each
row reverses direction and connects to the next through a U-turn arc. This
compact layout lets you compare many items at once while preserving
adjacency information such as inter-item correlations.

The package ships with three datasets from an experience sampling study of
university students (Neubauer & Schmiedek, 2024), rescaled to a 1--5 Likert
scale, and 10 built-in color palettes via `snake_palette()`. The bundled
scales have five levels, so every palette below is interpolated to
`n = 5`; a palette passed with more colors than levels would only use its
first five.

```{r load}
library(snakeplot)

labs5 <- c("1" = "Not at all", "2" = "Slightly", "3" = "Moderate",
           "4" = "Quite",      "5" = "Extremely")
```

## Daily EMA — value distribution ticks

Beep-level data hides day-to-day change once it is averaged per person.
Giving `survey_snake()` the raw beeps with `var` and `day` keeps one band
per day, so a shift in the response distribution across the study period
is visible band by band. Ticks are positioned within proportional zones by
response level, so the width of each colored zone is the share of beeps
at that level on that day:

```{r daily_value, fig.height = 8}
survey_snake(ema_beeps, var = "angry", day = "day",
             colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5), level_labels = labs5,
             title = "Anger — 14 days, value distribution")
```

## Daily EMA — distribution bars

Ticks show individual beeps; bars trade that detail for exact shares.
With `tick_shape = "bar"` each day becomes a stacked percentage bar, which
is the better choice when the question is how much of each day sits at the
top of the scale. `bar_reverse = TRUE` starts each bar at the highest
level:

```{r daily_bars, fig.height = 8}
survey_snake(ema_beeps, var = "happy", day = "day",
             tick_shape = "bar", bar_reverse = TRUE,
             colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5), level_labels = labs5,
             title = "Happiness — 14 days, distribution bars")
```

## Activity timelines

A week of time-stamped events is hard to read as one long axis.
`activity_snake()` gives each day its own band on a shared clock (6AM to
midnight by default), so habits such as late-night activity line up across
days. Events with zero duration appear as rug ticks on a dark ribbon:

```{r activity, fig.height = 6}
set.seed(42)
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
d <- data.frame(
  day      = rep(days, each = 40),
  start    = round(runif(280, 360, 1400)),
  duration = 0
)
activity_snake(d)
```

Pass character timestamps directly — they are parsed automatically:

```{r flex_activity, fig.height = 6}
set.seed(42)
dates <- seq(as.POSIXct("2024-03-11"), as.POSIXct("2024-03-17"),
             by = "day")
events <- data.frame(
  timestamp = format(
    rep(dates, each = 30) + round(runif(210, 6*3600, 22*3600)),
    "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
activity_snake(events, title = "From character timestamps — 7 days")
```

Duration blocks show event length as filled rectangles:

```{r activity_blocks, fig.height = 6}
set.seed(42)
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
d2 <- data.frame(
  day      = rep(days, each = 8),
  start    = round(runif(56, 360, 1200)),
  duration = round(runif(56, 15, 120))
)
activity_snake(d2, event_color = "#e09480", band_color = "#3d2518",
               title = "Weekly activity — duration blocks")
```

With `flow = "natural"`, all bands read 6AM to 12AM left-to-right, with no
alternating. Compare: the default boustrophedon flips morning events
between left and right on alternate rows, while natural keeps them
consistently on the left:

```{r activity_natural, fig.height = 6}
set.seed(1)
d_morning <- data.frame(
  day      = rep(days, each = 15),
  start    = round(runif(105, 360, 720)),
  duration = 0
)
activity_snake(d_morning, flow = "natural",
               title = "Morning events — flow='natural' (6AM always left)")
```

## Line snake

When the measure is continuous (a sensor reading, a count per interval)
rather than a set of events, `line_snake()` draws it as a line winding
through the bands, so the daily rhythm and its day-to-day changes sit in one
panel:

```{r line_snake}
set.seed(42)
hours <- seq(0, 1440, by = 10)
d_line <- data.frame(
  day   = rep(c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"), each = length(hours)),
  time  = rep(hours, 5),
  value = sin(rep(hours, 5) / 1440 * 4 * pi) * 50 + 50 +
          rnorm(5 * length(hours), 0, 8)
)
line_snake(d_line, fill_color = "#e74c3c")
```

## Timeline snake

A career or project history is a small number of long phases.
`timeline_snake()` takes a 3-column data.frame (role, start, end),
expands it into monthly blocks and labels each transition date and each
band's year, so the length of each phase can be compared at a glance:

```{r timeline_snake}
career <- data.frame(
  role  = c("Intern", "Junior Dev", "Mid Dev",
            "Senior Dev", "Tech Lead", "Architect"),
  start = c("2015-01", "2015-07", "2017-01",
            "2019-07", "2022-07", "2024-01"),
  end   = c("2015-06", "2016-12", "2019-06",
            "2022-06", "2023-12", "2024-12")
)
timeline_snake(career,
               title = "Software Engineer — Career Path (2015-2024)")
```

## Tick lines with correlation arcs

Sorting items by their mean places similar items next to each other, and
`arc_fill = "correlation"` prints the Pearson *r* between each pair of
adjacent items at the U-turn that joins them. The arcs therefore show
whether items with similar means also move together across respondents:

```{r corr, fig.height = 7}
survey_snake(ema_emotions, tick_shape = "line",
             arc_fill = "correlation", sort_by = "mean",
             colors = snake_palette("berry", n = 5), level_labels = labs5,
             title = "Emotions — correlations at U-turns")
```

## Dot plot with dark bands

Dots with vertical jitter show each respondent separately, which reveals
clusters that ticks can hide. `band_palette` sets the band shading
gradient; a dark ramp makes the dots stand out:

```{r dots_dark, fig.height = 7}
survey_snake(ema_emotions, tick_shape = "dot", sort_by = "mean",
             colors = snake_palette("viridis", n = 5), level_labels = labs5,
             band_palette = c("#1a1228", "#1a2a42"),
             title = "Emotions — dots on dark bands")
```

## Mean and median markers

On a skewed item the mean and the median part ways. A diamond marks the
item mean and a dashed line the median, so items where a few extreme
responses pull the mean away from the typical answer stand out:

```{r markers, fig.height = 7}
survey_snake(ema_emotions, tick_shape = "bar", sort_by = "mean",
             show_mean = TRUE, show_median = TRUE,
             colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5), level_labels = labs5,
             title = "Emotions — mean (diamond) and median (dashed)")
```

## Faceted multi-construct

A multi-construct survey is easier to read one construct at a time. When
column names share a prefix (e.g., `Emo_`, `Mot_`), `facet = TRUE`
auto-groups them into panels, one per construct, and strips the prefix from
the item labels:

```{r facet, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 11}
survey_snake(student_survey, facet = TRUE, facet_ncol = 2L,
             tick_shape = "bar", sort_by = "mean",
             colors = snake_palette("earth", n = 5), level_labels = labs5)
```

## Survey sequence

When only the response shares matter, `survey_sequence()` drops the
individual ticks and draws each item as a 100% stacked bar with the
percentage printed in each segment wide enough to hold it. Raw responses
are tabulated automatically:

```{r survey_seq}
survey_sequence(ema_emotions, colors = snake_palette("earth", n = 5))
```

Matrix with row/col names — labels and levels are inferred automatically:

```{r flex_survey, fig.height = 6}
m <- matrix(c(50, 120, 80, 30,
              40,  90, 110, 60,
              70, 100,  70, 50,
              80,  85,  95, 40,
              30, 110,  90, 70,
              60,  75, 105, 55,
              45, 130,  65, 35), nrow = 7, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(c("Satisfaction", "Engagement", "Motivation",
                              "Belonging", "Autonomy", "Competence",
                              "Wellbeing"),
                            c("Low", "Medium", "High", "Very High")))
survey_sequence(m, title = "Labels from matrix dimnames",
                colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 4))
```

## Sequential distribution

A diverging palette implies a neutral midpoint. For ordinal scales without
one (frequency scales such as "Never" to "Always"), `sequential_dist()`
draws the same stacked bars in a single-hue ramp:

```{r seq_dist}
sequential_dist(ema_emotions)
```

## Sequence snake

A long categorical sequence (for example, the actions in a learning
session) does not fit on one line. `sequence_snake()` folds it into rows,
one block per time point colored by its state, and keeps the blocks flowing
through the arcs so the order is never broken:

```{r sequence_snake}
set.seed(42)
verbs <- c("Read", "Write", "Discuss", "Listen",
           "Search", "Plan", "Code", "Review")
# 40 runs of 1-4 repeats each, cut to the first 75 steps
runs <- replicate(40, rep(sample(verbs, 1), sample(4, 1)), simplify = FALSE)
seq75 <- head(unlist(runs), 75)
sequence_snake(seq75, title = "75-step learning sequence")
```

Pass a data.frame directly — the first character/factor column is
auto-detected:

```{r flex_df}
set.seed(1)
logs <- data.frame(
  id     = 1:80,
  action = sample(c("Read", "Write", "Discuss", "Search", "Code",
                     "Plan", "Review", "Listen"), 80, replace = TRUE)
)
sequence_snake(logs, rows = 5,
               title = "From a data.frame — column auto-detected")
```

## Built-in palettes

10 palettes are available by name through `snake_palette()`, five
diverging (for scales with a neutral midpoint) and five sequential:

```{r palette_names}
names(snake_palettes)
```

Use any palette by name:

```r
snake_palette("sunset", n = 5)  # interpolate to 5 colors
survey_snake(ema_emotions, colors = snake_palette("earth", n = 5),
             tick_shape = "bar")
```
